title: Four big multiplications with the suggested identity
description: Each of four multiplications is done with the identity the book suggests, by splitting a number near a round number. The board puts every answer back against the question by its last digit.
teaching_notes: One idea: choose the identity the book names, split near a round number, and build the answer from its parts. Watch for students who forget the middle part of a square, or who use the wrong round number for the sum times take away rule.

source: Figure it Out (identities and patterns, question 1)
video_script.why: The child can check an expansion, but has not yet chosen a round number and an identity to do a big multiplication.
video_script.substitution: Pick the identity the book names for each item, split the numbers near a round number, and build each answer from its parts, as the cards in the book did.
video_script.anchor: the four items of the book's question, each with its suggested identity
video_script.payoff_line: The last multiplication, forty three times forty five, is one thousand nine hundred thirty five.

final_answer.spoken: two thousand one hundred sixteen, one hundred fifty nine thousand nine hundred ninety one, eight thousand two hundred eighty one, one thousand nine hundred thirty five

maths_rules: last digits: 6×6 = 36 ends in 6; 7×3 = 21 ends in 1; 1×1 = 1; 3×5 = 15 ends in 5
video_script.design: One idea: pick the identity, split near a round number, build the answer from its parts. The three rule cards stay on the stage. The last multiplication is left before its final subtraction until the answer.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='four'/>It has four items. Forty six squared, and ninety one squared. Then three hundred ninety seven times four hundred three, and forty three times forty five.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Can we find all four without a long multiplication?

beats.on_screen: the four item cards stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: three rule cards: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a - b)² = a² - 2ab + b², (a + b)(a - b) = a² - b²

marks.sum: the rule card (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² appears
marks.take: the rule card (a - b)² = a² - 2ab + b² appears
marks.both: the rule card (a + b)(a - b) = a² - b² appears

beats.colours: the three terms of each rule in three colours
narration: <bookmark mark='sum'/>Your book gave three rules. A sum squared is eigh squared plus two eigh b plus b squared.
<bookmark mark='take'/>A take away squared is eigh squared minus two eigh b plus b squared.
<bookmark mark='both'/>A sum times a take away is eigh squared minus b squared.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the four items from your book.

beats.on_screen: To find: the value of each item, using its identity

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find each value with the identity the book suggests.

marks.sum: the parts are added to give 2116

beats.colours: the three terms in three colours
narration: <bookmark mark='split'/>Step one, use the square of a sum for forty six squared. Split forty six as forty plus six.
<bookmark mark='parts'/>Forty squared is one thousand six hundred. Twice forty times six is four hundred eighty. Six squared is thirty six.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Adding the three parts, forty six squared is two thousand one hundred sixteen.

marks.rule: the sum times take away rule is named

beats.colours: the sum and the take away in two colours
narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step two, use the sum times take away rule for three hundred ninety seven times four hundred three.
<bookmark mark='split'/>Write them as four hundred minus three, and four hundred plus three.
<bookmark mark='squares'/>Four hundred squared is one hundred sixty thousand, and three squared is nine.
<bookmark mark='take'/>Subtracting, the answer is one hundred fifty nine thousand nine hundred ninety one.

beats.colours: the three terms in three colours
narration: <bookmark mark='split'/>Step three, use the square of a take away for ninety one squared. Split ninety one as one hundred minus nine.
<bookmark mark='parts'/>One hundred squared is ten thousand. Twice one hundred times nine is one thousand eight hundred. Nine squared is eighty one.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Ten thousand minus one thousand eight hundred plus eighty one is eight thousand two hundred eighty one.

marks.rule: the sum times take away rule is named
marks.squares: 44² = 1936 and 1² = 1 appear, with the subtraction not yet worked out

beats.colours: the sum and the take away in two colours
narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step four, use the sum times take away rule for forty three times forty five.
<bookmark mark='split'/>The middle number is forty four. Write them as forty four minus one, and forty four plus one.
<bookmark mark='squares'/>Forty four squared is one thousand nine hundred thirty six, and one squared is one.

narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step five, put the answers back against the question, by the last digit. Six times six is thirty six, and the first answer ends in six.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Seven times three is twenty one, and the second answer ends in one.
<bookmark mark='third'/>One times one is one, and the third answer ends in one.
<bookmark mark='fourth'/>Three times five is fifteen, so the last answer must end in five.

marks.one: the first two answers are written in a row
marks.two: the third answer is written, and the row is boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The last multiplication, forty three times forty five, is one thousand nine hundred thirty five.
<bookmark mark='one'/>The first answer is two thousand one hundred sixteen. The second is one hundred fifty nine thousand nine hundred ninety one.
<bookmark mark='two'/>The third is eight thousand two hundred eighty one.
